group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 49-year-old woman with a background of biopsy-proven primary biliary cholangitis followed in hepatology clinic and longstanding systolic dysfunction attributed to a remote viral myocarditis presented to the emergency department in late spring after three days of worsening cough productive of thick, yellow sputum, subjective fever with rigors, and pleuritic discomfort along the right flank that forced her to sleep upright the prior night. She lives with her partner in a single-family home, commutes to work as a graphic designer, selects and prepares her own meals, and denies any recent travel, incarceration, or stays in rehabilitation or extended-care facilities. She takes carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily, and ursodiol 600 mg daily, and reports excellent adherence. No loop diuretic has been required for over a year, and her last transthoracic echocardiogram six months earlier noted an ejection fraction of 40 % without significant valvular pathology. She has never been told she has chronic kidney disease, has had normal serum creatinine on routine panels, and denies hematuria, frothy urine, or edema at baseline. She has not been hospitalized in the past two years and has received no antibiotics since an episode of acute sinusitis eighteen months ago. On arrival she was sitting upright on the stretcher, flushed but conversant, answering questions appropriately, and oriented to date, location, and situation. Vital signs recorded before any antipyretics, fluids, or oxygen supplementation showed an oral temperature of 38.8 °C, pulse 89 beats per minute and regular, blood pressure 115/68 mm Hg in the left arm, respiratory rate 33 breaths per minute with shallow excursions and mild use of accessory musculature, and an oxygen saturation fluctuating between 89 % and 91 % while breathing room air. She spoke in short sentences but did not appear confused or somnolent. Conjunctiva were injected but anicteric; sclerae were white. Jugular venous pressure was not elevated at 45°. Cardiac examination revealed a displaced but nondiffuse point of maximal impulse, soft S3 consistent with chronic cardiomyopathy, and no new murmurs or pericardial rub. Pulmonary auscultation disclosed diminished breath sounds with coarse crackles over the right mid- and lower-posterior lung fields; percussion in the same region was dull, and tactile fremitus was decreased near the costophrenic angle. Abdomen was soft with a palpable, nodular but nontender liver edge two centimeters below the costal margin; no ascites or spider angiomata were evident. Extremities were warm with brisk capillary refill and no peripheral edema. Neurologic screening showed fluent speech, intact cranial nerves II-XII, 5/5 strength throughout, normal sensation, and steady finger-to-nose testing. A finger-stick glucose performed at triage was 130 mg/dL. Laboratory studies drawn prior to any therapy revealed sodium 131 mEq/L, potassium 3.9 mEq/L, chloride 100 mEq/L, bicarbonate 23 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 23 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, and hematocrit 46 %. Aspartate aminotransferase was 68 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 54 U/L, albumin 3.4 g/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.3, consistent with her known cholestatic liver disease. White blood cell count measured 14.0 × 10⁹/L with 86 % neutrophils, and platelet count was normal. An arterial blood gas obtained on room air showed pH 7.47, PaCO₂ 34 mm Hg, PaO₂ 73 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 24 mEq/L. Point-of-care lactate was 1.9 mmol/L. A portable upright chest radiograph demonstrated a dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms accompanied by blunting of the right costophrenic angle and a small meniscus sign suggesting an early parapneumonic effusion; cardiomediastinal silhouette was unchanged from outpatient imaging two months earlier and pulmonary vasculature was not congested. Electrocardiogram revealed sinus rhythm at 88 beats per minute with nonspecific intraventricular conduction delay but no acute ischemic changes. Ultrasonography of the thorax performed at the bedside showed a hypoechoic stripe layering above the right hemidiaphragm measuring approximately 8 mm, confirming a small fluid collection, and B-lines emanating from the consolidated parenchyma. No kidney abnormalities or hydronephrosis were identified on the limited abdominal sweep. Prior to blood draw she had not ingested analgesics or antipyretics that day, and no intravenous fluids, bronchodilators, diuretics, or antimicrobials had been started at the time of the above measurements.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) adds demographic, comorbidity, examination, and test-result points using pretreatment findings.
1. Demographics: For a woman, start with age minus 10: 49 − 10 = 39. She lives at home, so nursing-home residence adds 0.
2. Comorbidities: Chronic liver disease (primary biliary cholangitis) adds 20; chronic systolic heart failure adds 10. No malignancy, cerebrovascular disease, or renal disease is reported: 0 each.
3. Examination: Respiratory rate 33/min meets the ≥30 threshold: +20. She is oriented, systolic BP is 115 mm Hg (not <90), temperature is 38.8 °C (neither <35 nor ≥40), and pulse is 89/min (not ≥125): 0 each.
4. Tests: Pleural effusion adds 10. Arterial pH 7.47 is not <7.35, BUN 23 is not ≥30 mg/dL, sodium 131 is not <130 mEq/L, glucose 130 is not ≥250 mg/dL, and hematocrit 46% is not <30%: 0 each. Using the measured room-air PaO₂ of 73 mm Hg, the <60 mm Hg oxygenation criterion scores 0.
Total = 39 + 20 + 10 + 20 + 10 = 99 (risk class IV).
Final answer: 99
